newsitem.title: USA: US says child deaths from air bags rising.
newsitem.headline: US says child deaths from air bags rising.

text.p: The number of children killed by front-seat passenger air bags has escalated sharply, with 18 deaths this year, up from eight in 1995, five in 1994 and just one in 1993, federal officials said on Thursday.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) report stressed the value of air bags in preventing crash injuries and deaths when lap and shoulder safety belts are worn but it said children are safer in a vehicle's back seat.

"It's always been recommended that kids ride in the back seat and they're safer in every circumstance if they are belted in the back seat," CDC epidemiologist Julie Bolen said. "We can prevent any more child deaths if we do that."

Of the 32 children killed by air bags since 1993, the CDC said 21 were not wearing lap and shoulder safety belts. Nine infants less than a year old were in a child-safety seat facing away from the dashboard. Two 5-year-olds died while wearing lap and shoulder safety belts in the front seat.

The rise in child deaths from air bags corresponds with an increase in the number of cars equipped with them. In 1993, about 1.4 million vehicles had passenger-side air bags. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimated the number rose to 21.6 million vehicles this year.
The NHTSA said air bags have saved more than 1,500 lives, reducing driver fatalities 11 percent in passenger cars, including a 30 percent drop in deaths in head-on collisions.
"Air bags, when they're combined with lap and shoulder belts save lots of lives and prevent lots of injuries," Bolen said.
-- Infants under a year old never ride in the front seat of a vehicle with a passenger-side air bag.
-- Children under age 12 always ride in the back seat.
-- All vehicle occupants wear lap and shoulder belts.

The NHTSA has proposed that vehicles equipped with passenger-side air bags carry these warnings on the sun visor: "Children 12 and under can be killed by the air bag" and "Never put a rear-facing child seat in the front."
Starting in the 1998 model year all passenger cars must have dual air bags. The requirement covers light trucks beginning with the 1999 model year.
